title: Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation would turn an existing software system into a reviewable account of its behavior: modular contracts describing its components, interfaces, dependencies, and constraints, together with machine-checked evidence that the legacy implementation satisfies those contracts. It would explicitly identify the behavior and proof obligations left unresolved. The purpose is to make those recovered contracts useful enough to support verified repairs and replacements, including systems whose important behavior was never formally documented.

As a synthesis of the target capability, sound recovery means that accepted claims follow under stated programming-language semantics and environment assumptions. It does not require recovering every property of every program. A useful result must distinguish proved contracts, assumptions, and an explicit residual of unproved obligations. Recovering behavior also does not establish that the behavior is desirable: undocumented bugs and historical conventions may be part of what a replacement must preserve or deliberately change.

significance.text: Legacy modernization faces a concrete compatibility problem: enhancements or replacements can fail to compose safely with the surrounding system, while formal specifications needed for verified construction may be unavailable. Sound recovery at production scale could replace substantial manual reconstruction with human-auditable contracts and checkable conformance arguments. Its revolutionary contribution would be making verified component replacement practical for systems that were not originally developed around formal contracts.

The compatibility guarantee requires more than proving properties of the old code. The replacement must also satisfy the recovered contract, and that contract must constrain the observations that matter to callers and the surrounding system. Preserving selected invariants can establish preservation of those properties without establishing full behavioral equivalence. The Daikon and ESC/Java integration work describes checking modifications against previously inferred and checked specifications, providing a limited predecessor to this mechanism.

Conditional downstream possibilities include safer modernization of financial and safety-critical software, replacement of obsolete components, and more deliberate separation of required compatibility from behavior that should change. These are prospective consequences, not demonstrated sector-wide outcomes. Guarantees would remain conditional on the modeled language, dependencies, environment, and trusted verification components. Physical-system safety, fitness for intended use, and regulatory acceptance would require additional evidence; assumptions about the physical environment must be stated explicitly rather than hidden inside an unrestricted residual.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is a useful, sound, scalable integration of specification recovery and verification. It must infer modular contracts strong enough to verify designated replacements, establish that the legacy system satisfies them, and expose remaining obligations. DARPA's V-SPELLS goals identify central engineering challenges: recovering architecture and domain models, making interfaces and dependencies explicit, automating specification inference, and enabling developers to compose verified new components safely with existing code.

Execution-based inference alone cannot supply the guarantee. A property that holds in observed runs may fail on an untested execution, so inferred candidates require further justification. Combining dynamic inference with static checking is already a demonstrated idea; the unresolved integration challenge includes establishing the assumptions used by the checker and obtaining enough verified properties to support meaningful replacement. In the RV'01 prototype, some ownership annotations were introduced without source analysis and could be unsafe, illustrating how apparently helpful proof inputs can weaken an end-to-end assurance claim.

General limits on static inference also matter: the reviewed TSE material discusses true properties that cannot be computed and properties dependent on how a program is used, including its inputs. This supports bounded recovery under explicit assumptions, but it does not establish a precise impossibility theorem for an unspecified task called exact inference. The scientific problem must identify the property language, program class, and desired guarantees before a specific undecidability claim can be evaluated.

As an engineering synthesis, success must balance soundness, contract strength, modularity, and cost. A weak contract can be easy to prove yet inadequate for compatibility; an enormous residual can conceal almost all useful behavior. Conversely, contracts too detailed or expensive to understand and maintain may defeat the modernization purpose. The supplied historical evidence motivates these challenges but does not establish whether the full target capability remains unavailable as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The supplied DARPA V-SPELLS page marks the program complete and states that the page is no longer maintained. It describes a developer-accessible approach to incremental enhancement of legacy software, including inferred architecture and domain models, specification inference, and safe composition of verified components. Its resulting-tools section lists a demonstration of Taphos, Oxide, and Walrus. The reviewed page does not claim sound behavioral recovery of an entire production system; that absence on this page does not establish that no such result exists elsewhere.

Nimmer and Ernst's RV'01 preliminary paper reports combining Daikon's dynamic invariant inference with ESC/Java static checking on small programs. Dynamic inference proposes properties from executions, and the paper explicitly recognizes that these candidates need not hold over every possible execution. Subsequent static checking is a meaningful achievement beyond mining alone. However, the prototype's potentially unsafe ownership annotations prevent its reported checks from establishing the stronger end-to-end sound recovery envisaged here. This limitation narrows the result's guarantee without negating the reported experiments.

Ernst, Cockrell, Griswold, and Notkin reported accurate and useful invariant inference, at least for small programs, in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 27(2), pages 99–123, February 2001. The supplied review supports this scoped conclusion from the abstract and discusses inference limits from the associated paper. The abstract is a partial representation of the publication, and extraction of the retained full-paper text truncates on page 23; the relevant discussion of static-inference limits was available before that truncation. These materials support a dated, limited result rather than production-scale recovery.

The research also cites Lathouwers and Huisman's 2024 Survey of annotation generators for deductive verifiers and attributes to it a conclusion that generated specifications fall far short of a deductive-verification baseline. No captured text for this source was supplied, so that conclusion and the document's identity could not be assessed in the review. It remains an unverified attribution in this record, not an established finding or evidence that the survey is wrong.

The supplied record contains no freshness search with which to assess the frontier as of November 1, 2026. The historical experiments and completed-program description establish motivation and partial predecessors, but they establish neither achievement nor present-day absence of the proposed integrated capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: demonstrate the method on a production system of at least one million lines, or a smaller system with documented regulatory evidence that rewriting is prohibitively costly. Produce a human-reviewable modular specification, a machine-checked legacy conformance proof covering a predeclared substantial subset, and a clean-room reimplementation checked against the same recovered contract. The size threshold, regulatory alternative, and clean-room requirement are proposed evaluation choices, not published standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Million-line or regulatory-alternative conformance proof and clean-room replacement

completion_criteria.text: Before evaluation, define the observations that constitute compatibility, the language semantics, environment and dependency assumptions, trusted components, minimum contract coverage, and an acceptably bounded residual with explicit outstanding obligations. Explain why the recovered contracts are strong enough for the designated replacement task. Report environmental assumptions separately from unproved implementation behavior, so a successful proof cannot conceal its limits through an unconstrained residual.
completion_criteria.label: Assumptions separated from unproved behavior, bounded residual, replacement justification

completion_criteria.text: A proposed pre-registered differential suite should exercise declared interfaces and operating conditions, with any observed disagreements confined to the stated residual. Such testing would corroborate the proofs and help reveal modeling or integration mistakes; it cannot prove that every possible disagreement is confined to that residual. Evaluation across multiple systems would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested domains, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered differential suite confines disagreements to the stated residual

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, independent evaluators should be able to rerun the recovery process and proof checks from the evaluated code, configurations, assumptions, and tool versions. Report human annotation effort, recovery and checking costs, unresolved obligations, and the boundary of the trusted verification machinery. Developers who are not verification experts should then replace a subsystem using the recovered interfaces and verify the replacement against its contract. This proposed usability test would show whether the recovered knowledge supports practical maintenance rather than only an expert-led demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Independent rerun, full recovery accounting, and non-expert verified replacement

related_concepts.text: The following relationships are conceptual interpretations of the supplied roster titles, whose full definitions were not supplied. SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems, overlaps directly in legacy modernization. SWE-06 reconstructs useful contracts and checks legacy conformance; SWE-11 concerns preservation of behavior through transformation under defined semantics. Recovery can support transformation, but transformation can also rely on direct equivalence arguments or language semantics without a separately recovered specification. SWE-01, Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems, similarly concerns assurance across a compilation step rather than discovering a legacy system's modular contracts.

SWE-02, Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications, could consume recovered contracts to construct replacements, provided those contracts are adequate for the task. SWE-03, Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment, addresses a separate obligation: determining whether a specification captures what is wanted and the relevant operating world. SWE-06 establishes what legacy code satisfies under stated assumptions; that alone cannot establish intended correctness.

SWE-04, A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail, and SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries, concern reasoning about interacting components. Recovered contracts could supply inputs to such reasoning, while those concepts could help establish system-level consequences of component guarantees. SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change, concerns maintaining assurance as software evolves; recovered interfaces and obligations could provide a starting point, but efficient ongoing assurance is a distinct capability.

SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs, could help enforce boundaries around a component with incompletely recovered behavior, but confinement would not explain that behavior or prove replacement compatibility. SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution, and SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code, concern particular execution guarantees that recovery might seek to characterize. Establishing either guarantee would not by itself recover the wider contract of a legacy system.

change_log.change: Preserved SWE-06's identity while defining the target as useful, sound recovery integrated with verification at production scale.
change_log.reason: The reviewed sources already demonstrate limited inference and checking; novelty cannot rest on the first recovery or verification of any property.

change_log.change: Replaced claims of present-day absence and a largely unspecified installed base with bounded historical evidence and an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources do not quantify prevalence or establish the frontier as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Made replacement conformance and sufficiently strong observable contracts explicit conditions of compatibility.
change_log.reason: Legacy conformance and preservation of selected properties alone do not prove that a replacement preserves all relevant behavior.

change_log.change: Separated environmental assumptions, trusted components, and unproved residual obligations.
change_log.reason: These impose different limits on the guarantee and should not be collapsed into an unrestricted residual.

change_log.change: Reframed the broad exact-inference undecidability assertion as a need for a precisely defined inference problem.
change_log.reason: The reviewed material supports general computability limitations but not the original unspecified theorem-like assertion.

change_log.change: Integrated the small-program Daikon and ESC/Java results and their potentially unsafe ownership annotations.
change_log.reason: Both the demonstrated predecessor and the limitation on its assurance are necessary to characterize progress fairly.

change_log.change: Preserved the dated 2001 result, publication details, and relevant extraction limitations; qualified the uncaptured 2024 survey attribution.
change_log.reason: Supported historical findings should remain, while unavailable source content cannot substantiate the attributed conclusion.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed evaluation with substantial predeclared coverage, bounded residuals, replacement checking, reproducibility, and practical effort reporting.
change_log.reason: These make success meaningful and reviewable while retaining the original production-scale and nonexpert-developer goals.

change_log.change: Clarified that differential testing provides empirical corroboration and finite evaluations establish demonstrated breadth.
change_log.reason: Neither establishes universal compatibility beyond the formal guarantee and its assumptions.

change_log.change: Corrected the claimed prerequisite relationship to SWE-11 and related SWE-06 to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Verified transformation does not universally require recovered specifications, and roster titles support only provisional conceptual comparisons.

unresolved_issues: Whether the integrated capability has been demonstrated at useful production scale as of November 1, 2026 remains unassessed because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The cited 2024 survey's identity, scope, and attributed conclusion remain unverified because no captured text was supplied.
A precise inference problem is needed before attaching a specific undecidability result to the target capability.
The proposed evaluation still requires operational definitions of substantial coverage, sufficient contract strength, acceptable residual size, and practical cost.
Full definitions of the related roster concepts were not supplied; their relationships are interpretations of titles, particularly the candidate-specific scope of SWE-11.
The associated 2001 TSE paper's retained extraction is truncated, limiting conclusions about material beyond the passages covered by the supplied review.
